y ~ 0 + region + (1|year:region)

I have been struggling to find a syntax within f() that does this.

Kind regards,

Christoph

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 2014-03-06 at 23:45 -0800, Anne Louise Nielsen wrote:
> Hi
>
>
> I noticed from the output from my use of INLA that the output contains
> "expected number of effective parameters". When you compute the DIC,
> i.e. dic=TRUE the "effective number of parameters" is also computed. I
> know that the latter is used for the calculation of the DIC. My
> question is, why are these two numbers of parameters different, and
> what is the difference between them?
>
>
> BR
> Anne Louise

good question. the effective number of parameters you see in the
summary(result), uses the approximation

 p_D = p - trace( -P * V)

where P is the prior precision matrix and V is the posterior covariance
matrix (refer to the DIC) paper.

The effective number of parameters in result$dic, is computed using
p_D = mean(deviance) - deviance(mean), again refer to the DIC paper.
(well, deviance(mean) uses the mode of the hyperparameters and the mean
of the latent field.)

the two numbers are usually in agreement but for more non-Gaussian data
they can disagree a little. the p_D in the $dic is more accurate. the
reason for doing like this, is that the approximation is cheap to
compute (in fact, almost free), whereas the other one is much more
expensive. also, p_D just give a rough guideline of the effective
number of parameters, as the hole DIC concept is somewhat
approximate...

Best
H

messages.subject_clean: Hyperparameters for rw1 and SPDE models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am new to INLA but am hoping to use it for species distribution modelling. I have built a model that works fine using environmental covariates, but I want to include a distance-based covariate to check for point clustering. I have used this Illian 2013 paper as a guide:

http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210x.12017/full

The paper warns that it is important to consider the hyperparameters for spatial effects and the distance covariate (referred to as a "constructed covariate" in the paper), or else the signal from the fixed environmental covariates could be lost. Unfortunately, that appears to be the case for me. I have fitted a model with 14 environmental covariates, of which 12 are significantly different from 0. When I include the distance covariate using the "rw1" model, however, this number drops to 3. There is no indication of how to select the hyperparameters in the paper of appendix, and as a newbie to Bayesian methods, I seem to have hit a wall. I have tried playing around with different hyperparameters as well as other arguments such as scale.model and inla.group but it has been to no avail thus far. Furthermore, I've also tried to model the latent Gaussian field using an SPDE model, and a similar culling of significant variables happens.

Does anyone have any guidelines for choosing the hyperparameters of the "rw1" model and the SPDE model?

Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Ian

messages.body_plain:
It does not make sense to have
      f(id, as.factor(x), model='iid')
because the second argument in f() must be numeric

Also, I think that
       y ~ factor(x)
is more or less the same as
       y ~ f(x, model='iid')
So, by having
       y ~ factor(x) + f(x, model='iid')
we have a redundancy and identification problem as well.

You can see that
   inla(y ~ factor(x))$summary.fix
is similar to
   inla(y ~ f(x, model='iid'))$summary.random$x

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

dev.new <http://dev.new>() is needed whenever one needs multiple plots visible at the same time, which is not at all an unreasonable thing to want. Yes, a new virtual "device" will be open automatically without it, but it will replace the existing plot.  inla.dev.new <http://inla.dev.new>() is a workaround for the (in my opinion severly misguided) behaviour of RStudio that only allows a single "physical" device to be available.  While it would be nice to have an option in the plot(inla.result) to specify what behaviour the user wants, a cleaner method is to specifically plot each desired plot explicitly instead of relying on the "plot everything in a rudimentary way" behaviour of the simple plot command (for complex models; a _lot_ of figures are generated!).

Håvard may have other opinions and/or solutions...

Finn L

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Expectation at mesh nodes
messages.body_plain:
On 19/03/14 08:43, Jussi wrote:
> Is there a way to get expectation of a spatial model such as g(intercept
> + s), where g is inverse link function and s is spatial "random effect"
> at the mesh nodes? What I want to do is to feed the expectations for
> inla.mesh.project and find volume under the estimated spatial surface.

You seem to be asking for two different things, so let's clear things
up: Let u(x) be the intercept+spatial effect at location x.

The (submitted) tutorial text available at
   http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/papers/jss/lindgren.pdf
shows how to get the posteriors for intercept + spde model
into fitted.values in the output at arbitrary locations (just use
mesh$loc as coordinates to get the values at mesh nodes).
For small meshes an alternative is to use the "lincomb" feature instead.

Section 3.3 shows how to specify whether to apply a link function or
not.  See also the r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> FAQ entry about how to make predictions.

E(u(x)) is straightforward; no link specification needed, as any NA data
will not have a link function applied unless you specifically tell it to
do that.  fitted.values will contain the posterior distributions
for u(x) at the mesh nodes.

E(g(u(x))) is the same as E(u(x)) except that you need to tell it to
actually apply the link function to in the prediction.  fitted.values
will contain the posteriors for g(u(x)) at the mesh nodes.

Your final sentence seems to ask for

\int E( g(u(x)) ) dx

which is also easy once you have the gux=E(g(u(x))) result; simply evaluate
sum(gux * (inla.mesh.fem(mesh, order=1)$c1 %*% gux))
to get a simple integral approximation.

In order to get a better approximation you may want to do the
predictions of g(x(u)) on a slightly finer mesh than your model; this
is also straightforward: use fine.mesh$loc and
inla.mesh.fem(fine.mesh,...) above.  fitted.values will contain the
posteriors for g(u(x)) at the nodes of the fine mesh.
But the model itself will still be piecewise linear for x(s).

Finn L

You have to do those changes *within* the AnimalINLA package.
This means that you need to download the source, make the changes, and reinstall the package with your modifications.

I have done it. So you might want to benefit from that.
In fact, there were some other changes in the INLA syntaxis that were not translated to the AnimalINLA package.
Namely, inla.marginal.transform and inla.expectation are called now inla.tmarginal and inla.emarginal respectively.
I have changed those as well in my fixes.

You can proceed as follows:
install.packages('devtools')
library(devtools)
install_github('myAnimalINLAfixes', 'famuvie')

Now you have my little package with the modified version of the function animal.inla()
To use it, you simply load my package *after* AnimalINLA, which will override the original function.
library(AnimalINLA)
library(myAnimalINLAfixes)

Then you can use it.

Hope it helps.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm loving INLA, but have a (hopefully) simple question.

I'm looking at effects of no2 on binary outcomes by region, where the no2 effects are modified by regional income levels.

I have data for i=1,...,N (individuals) and j=1,...,J (census tract levels) with,

Individual binary outcomes y, of length N.
Individual exposures, no2, of length N.
Individual census tract indicator data, ct, of length N.
Census tract (ct) level income data, income, of size J.

I also easily create a "full" income vector of size N as, income.full = income[ct]

The model is:

logit(y) = alpha + beta*no2
where
beta = gamma_1 + gamma_2*income + error

I'm mainly interested in posteriors for region-level beta's.
I have fit this model in JAGS, lmer and INLA, getting nearly identical results for all three.  The INLA code is:

mod.inla <- inla(y ~ 1 + no2 + no2:income.full + f(ct,no2,model="iid"),family="binomial",data=dat.inla)
b.hat.inla <- mod.inla$summary.fixed["no2","mean"] + mod.inla$summary.fixed["no2:income.full","mean"] * income + mod.inla$summary.random$ct$mean

How can I get posterior distributions for the J beta's?  In particular I'm interested in mapping Pr(beta_j > 0) for each region j.

(Note: This is a first pass scaled down version of the model.  Of course I would like to add spatial smoothing effects on the beta's in time.)

Thanks!

John

Hi All,

I used the following code to create mesh, but the predicted mean map is not smooth in hotspots i.e has vertex corners as can be observed in the attached.

Is it possible to modify mesh inorder to achieve a smoother map. My model was AR2

mesh.dummy=inla.mesh.create(loc=borders,extend=list(n=10, offset=0.7),refine=FALSE)
boundary = inla.mesh.boundary(mesh.dummy)
mesh = inla.mesh.create(boundary=boundary,
                        refine=list(max.edge=0.5))
nmesh = mesh$n;nmesh
mesh.idx = mesh$idx$loc
plot(mesh)
lines(borders,lwd=3)
points(coordinates$Long,coordinates$Lat,pch=20,cex=2, col="blue")
points(coordinates.val$Long,coordinates.val$Lat,pch=20,cex=2, col="red")
points(boundary[[1]]$loc,col=3,cex=3,pch=20)

# ################################
## Make the SPDE object and the formula
## ################################

spde=inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh, alpha=2)

A.est=inla.spde.make.A(mesh,loc=as.matrix(coordinates[civ.data$Cluster_ID,c("Long","Lat")]),group=civ.data$time,n.group=no.years)

A.val=inla.spde.make.A(mesh,loc=as.matrix(coordinates.val[civ.validation$Cluster_ID,c("Long","Lat")]),group=civ.validation$time,n.group=no.years)

i.year<-31

A.pred<-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, group=i.year, n.group=no.years)
field.indices <-inla.spde.make.index("field",n.spde=mesh$n,n.group=no.years)

stack.est <-inla.stack(data=list(Pf=civ.data$Pf),A=list(A.est, 1),effects=list(c(field.indices, list(Intercept=1)),list(civ.data[,4:7])),tag="est")
stack.val<-inla.stack(data=list(Pf=NA),A=list(A.val,1),effects=list(c(field.indices,list(intercept=1)),list(civ.validation[,4:7])),tag="val")

scaled.mesh.loc<-list(Long=(rep(scale(mesh$loc[,1],mean.covariates["Long"],sd.covariates["Long"]),no.years)),Lat=(rep(scale(mesh$loc[,2],mean.covariates["Lat"],sd.covariates["Lat"]),no.years)))
stack.pred<-inla.stack(data=list(Pf=NA), A=list(A.pred),effects=list(c(field.indices,scaled.mesh.loc,list(Intercept=1) )),tag="pred")

stack<-inla.stack(stack.est, stack.val,stack.pred)
str(inla.stack.data(stack.est))
str(inla.stack.data(stack.val))
str(inla.stack.data(stack.pred))
str(inla.stack.data(stack))

formula=(Pf ~ -1 + Intercept + Long+ Lat + prec+urbanization + f(field, model = spde, group = field.group, control.group =list(model="ar",order=2)))
